prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Uber Technologies, Inc" (ticker UBER), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "UBER", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Uber Technologies, Inc.
result.industry: Ride-hailing, food and grocery delivery, and freight marketplaces
markets: Ride-hailing and urban mobility (Uber rides, taxis, rentals, autonomous rides)
Food, grocery and retail delivery (Uber Eats, Postmates, Trendyol Go)
Digital freight brokerage and logistics software (Uber Freight)
Membership and advertising (Uber One, Journey Ads)
Autonomous vehicle ride and fleet platform

mission.statement: We reimagine the way the world moves for the better
mission.source: Uber company website, About us page (uber.com/about)
mission.plain: Uber wants to make it easier and better for people and things to get around.

about.plain: Uber runs apps that connect people who need something moved with people who will move it. You can tap a button to get a ride in a stranger's car, or get dinner or groceries brought to your door. Uber does not own the cars or the restaurants; it takes a cut of each trip or order. It also helps trucking companies find loads to carry.
about.customers: Everyday riders and diners (202 million monthly users at the end of 2025), restaurants and stores that want deliveries, businesses that book travel and meals, and shippers that need trucks.
about.everyday: If you have ever hailed a ride home from the airport with your phone or had a burger delivered through Uber Eats, you have used Uber.

money.plain: rides in cars, taxis and robotaxis booked in the app
restaurant food, groceries and shop items brought to your door
matching shippers with truck drivers and logistics software
ads shown in the app and a monthly subscription for discounts (50 million members in Q1 2026)
robotaxi rides from partners such as Waymo, Wayve and Baidu on the Uber app

result.summary: Uber has a real competitive advantage from its two-sided network: it is the largest ride-hailing and number-two delivery platform outside China, with 13.6 billion trips and $193.5 billion of Gross Bookings in 2025, so riders get shorter waits and drivers get more jobs than on smaller rivals. Sharing drivers, users and the Uber One membership across rides and delivery lowers costs further. The advantage is not unassailable: local rivals (DoorDash, DiDi, Bolt, Grab, Meituan's Keeta) win in specific markets, and robotaxi companies such as Waymo and Tesla could bypass the driver network that underpins the moat.

pricingPower.evidence: Uber has steadily raised take rates and added fees while volumes kept growing (2025 trips +20%, Gross Bookings +19%) and moved from a $4.9 billion operating loss in 2020 to $5.6 billion operating income in 2025, but riders and eaters remain price-sensitive and multi-app; in Q2 2026 trip growth slowed, which Uber blamed on heavy spending by DiDi and Meituan in Brazil, and US share in delivery trails DoorDash.

moats.evidence: "Uber" is a verb for hailing a ride in many countries, and the app operates in over 70 countries and more than 15,000 cities; first-time users in Q2 2026 were the highest in five years.

Riders, eaters and drivers can install a rival app in seconds and many multi-home; Uber One (50 million members, about half of Mobility and Delivery Gross Bookings) adds some stickiness through discounts.

More riders attract more drivers, which shortens waits and raises earnings per hour; Uber had 202 million monthly active platform consumers at end-2025 and about 76% of observed US rideshare spending versus Lyft (Bloomberg Second Measure, March 2024).

Spreading $3.4 billion of R&D and shared driver supply over $193.5 billion of 2025 Gross Bookings lets Uber run at a 4.9% Adjusted EBITDA margin on bookings in Q2 2026, which smaller rivals like Lyft (an operating loss in 2025) struggle to match.
Most local ride-hailing markets support only one or two profitable networks, and Uber is number one or two in its core markets such as the US, UK and much of Latin America.
Uber's asset-light, gig-driver model once undercut taxis, but incumbents and new rivals now copy it, and Waymo's own app is counter-positioning against Uber with driverless fleets.
Over a decade of pricing, matching, routing and fraud-control data across billions of trips, plus cross-platform batching of rides and deliveries, is hard for new entrants to replicate quickly.
Uber owns no exclusive assets; drivers are independent and Waymo is ending its exclusive Uber arrangements in Austin and Atlanta by early 2028.

customers.evidence: Engagement is rising (monthly active platform consumers 208 million in Q2 2026, up 16%; trips 3.9 billion, up 18%) and Uber One reached 50 million members, but surveys of rideshare users regularly cite price surges and fees, and loyalty is limited because many users also use Lyft or DoorDash.

talent.evidence: Uber pays top-of-market tech salaries and has about 34,000 employees, and its reputation has recovered since the 2017 scandals under Dara Khosrowshahi, but it is not usually listed among the very top employer rankings and its driver relationships remain contentious (over 150,000 US drivers have filed or intended to file arbitration demands).

product.evidence: Uber offers the broadest single app for rides, delivery, groceries, rentals and robotaxi rides across 70+ countries, with features such as Uber One and cross-platform offers; it is widely regarded as the reference app in ride-hailing, though DoorDash is the leader in US food delivery.

competitors.name: Lyft
competitors.note: Number-two US and Canada ride-hailing network (51.3 million annual riders in 2025), also expanding into Europe through FreeNow.

competitors.name: DoorDash
competitors.note: US food delivery leader (about 61% of US delivery sales at end-2024 vs Uber Eats about 26%) and owner of Wolt and Deliveroo in Europe.

competitors.name: Waymo (Alphabet)
competitors.note: Leading robotaxi operator; partners with Uber in Austin and Atlanta but sells rides on its own app in San Francisco, Phoenix, Los Angeles and other cities.

competitors.name: Tesla
competitors.note: Building its own robotaxi network and ride app, a potential threat to Uber's driver-based model.

competitors.name: DiDi Global
competitors.note: China's ride-hailing leader, competing with Uber in Latin America (99 in Brazil), Australia and Japan, and pushing into Brazilian food delivery.

competitors.name: Bolt
competitors.note: Private Estonian ride-hailing and delivery app competing with Uber across Europe and Africa.

competitors.name: Grab Holdings
competitors.note: Southeast Asia's ride and delivery super-app (Uber sold its regional business to Grab in 2018 for a stake).

competitors.name: Meituan (Keeta)
competitors.note: China's delivery giant expanding its Keeta app into the Middle East and Brazil, competing with Uber Eats.

competitors.name: Instacart (Maplebear)
competitors.note: US grocery delivery leader competing with Uber Eats grocery.

competitors.name: Delivery Hero
competitors.note: Global delivery platform (Talabat, Baemin, Glovo); Uber launched a $14.8 billion all-cash takeover bid in July 2026 and already holds a large stake.

competitors.name: Amazon (Zoox)
competitors.note: Zoox robotaxis and Amazon's same-day retail delivery compete at the edges of Mobility and Delivery.

competitors.name: C.H. Robinson
competitors.note: Largest US freight broker, competing with Uber Freight.

competitors.name: RXO
competitors.note: US truckload brokerage competing with Uber Freight.

marketShare.market: US rideshare (share of observed Uber + Lyft consumer spending, Bloomberg Second Measure)
US online food delivery (Earnest Analytics, end of 2024)

threats: Robotaxi operators (Waymo, Tesla, Zoox) selling rides on their own apps instead of through Uber; Waymo is ending its exclusive Uber deals in Austin and Atlanta by early 2028.
Heavily funded Chinese rivals (DiDi's 99 and Meituan's Keeta) spending on rides and delivery in Brazil and the Middle East, which slowed Uber's trip growth in Q2 2026.
Driver classification and pay rules (EU Platform Work Directive, US state laws) and mass arbitration claims that could raise costs.
Execution and debt risk from the $14.8 billion all-cash Delivery Hero takeover, expected to close in the second half of 2027.
DoorDash's lead in US delivery and its expansion in Europe through Deliveroo and Wolt.
Large swings in GAAP profit from equity-stake revaluations and tax benefits, which make earnings quality harder to judge.

ceo.name: Dara Khosrowshahi
ceo.background: Electrical engineering degree from Brown University; former investment banker at Allen & Company and CEO of Expedia (2005-2017).

c1.evidence: Uber is the global leader (outside China) in app-based mobility, with $193.5 billion of Gross Bookings in 2025 growing 19%, and is positioning itself as the main platform for robotaxi rides.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Uber for its reliability and short waits from the largest driver network plus one app for rides and food, which is hard to copy at scale, but the advantage depends on human drivers and could erode if robotaxi fleets sell directly.

c3.evidence: "Uber" is a household name and verb, the default ride-hailing app in the US (about 76% of observed US rideshare spending vs Lyft), the UK and much of the world, though not in US food delivery where DoorDash leads.

c4.evidence: The mission "We reimagine the way the world moves for the better" is published, and Uber talks about AVs and electrification, but management under Khosrowshahi is best known for disciplined profit and buybacks ($6.5 billion repurchased in 2025) rather than a purpose-driven crusade.

c6.evidence: "convenient, ubiquitous, pricey"; the public sees Uber as indispensable and easy to use, with lingering negatives about surge pricing, fees, driver pay and its 2017-era culture, so the impression is mostly positive but mixed.

c7.evidence: Ride-hailing, delivery and freight are huge markets moving online, and Uber guides Q3 2026 Gross Bookings to grow 18-22% in constant currency, with autonomous vehicles as a further secular driver.

c8.evidence: Uber keeps expanding into groceries and retail delivery, advertising, Uber One memberships, robotaxis (target reported by the FT of about 120,000 driverless vehicles across 15+ cities) and, via the Delivery Hero bid, into Asia and the Middle East.

m1.evidence: Khosrowshahi articulates a clear plan to make Uber the largest platform for autonomous vehicles and a cross-platform everyday app, but he is seen more as a disciplined operator than a visionary founder.

m2.evidence: He is not a founder but has run Uber since 2017 with long-term moves such as AV partnerships and the Delivery Hero bid, while also focusing on near-term profitability.

m4.evidence: He rebuilt Uber's culture after the 2017 scandals with new values ("we do the right thing, period"), but relations with drivers over pay and classification remain strained.

m5.evidence: Uber launches many features each year (Uber One, Uber Reserve, teen accounts, AV Lab), but its culture is known for operational efficiency more than breakthrough invention, and it sold its own self-driving unit to Aurora in 2020.

m6.evidence: Khosrowshahi has an electrical engineering degree from Brown and is product-focused, but his career was in banking and running Expedia rather than engineering.

m7.evidence: He is widely regarded as having restored integrity at Uber after the Kalanick era, though there is no clear evidence his stewardship prioritises a cause beyond the business.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Khosrowshahi giving a commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university.

m8b.evidence: Khosrowshahi is known as a calm, diplomatic manager rather than a larger-than-life personality like Musk or Karp.

m9.evidence: Under him revenue rose from $11.1 billion in 2020 to $52.0 billion in 2025 and operating income swung from a $4.9 billion loss to $5.6 billion profit, with free cash flow reaching $9.8 billion in 2025.

m10.evidence: Uber has become cost-disciplined, holding R&D roughly flat ($3.2 billion in 2023, $3.4 billion in 2025) while revenue grew 40%, but it is not known for Bezos-style frugality.

c10.evidence: Uber's 13.6 billion trips in 2025 across 70+ countries give hundreds of millions of people easy rides and deliveries and millions of drivers and couriers flexible earnings.

p2.evidence: Running real-time marketplaces matching billions of trips is technically and operationally hard and important, but the core app has been copied by many regional rivals.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from -43.7% in 2020 to +10.7% in 2025, but reported gross margin (revenue less cost of revenue) fell from 53.7% to 39.8%, largely because of business model changes such as the UK where Uber books gross fares as revenue.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 debt was $12.7 billion against $5.4 billion of cash and short-term investments, but trailing free cash flow above $10 billion covers it and equity is a positive $28.2 billion.

f4.evidence: Operating income improved from -$4,863 million in 2020 to $5,565 million in 2025 and operating cash flow from -$2,745 million to $10,099 million, rising every year.

v1.evidence: In ride-hailing Uber is usually the best choice because its larger network means faster pickups almost everywhere you travel, but in US food delivery DoorDash has more restaurants and share, and robotaxi apps like Waymo offer a different alternative.

v2.evidence: Uber is a well-paying tech employer whose reputation has recovered since 2017, but no recent top employer ranking placing it near the top (e.g. Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For) was found.

c5.evidence: If Uber vanished, hundreds of millions of riders and diners, restaurants that rely on Uber Eats, and millions of drivers earning income would notice immediately, though Lyft, DoorDash and local rivals could absorb part of the demand.
